The union said the EFCC approached the university to establish an academy through which both institutions would share academic facilities and expertise, stressing that the arrangement did not confer ownership of the land on the anti-graft agency.
ASUU Chairman, University of Abuja Chapter, Prof. sylvanus Ugoh, stated this during an interview on Leadership Television’s Inside Nigeria, while responding to allegations by the Federal Capital Territory Administration (FCTA) that the university allocated portions of its land to organisations, including the EFCC, without approval.
Ugoh explained that the EFCC had approached the university to establish an academy, with lecturers from the institution expected to participate in training and academic activities.
He said the collaboration was designed to benefit both university students and EFCC personnel through shared knowledge and institutional resources.
According to him, the university had also considered similar collaborative arrangements with the Joint Admissions and Matriculation Board (JAMB) and the National Agency for Science and Engineering Infrastructure (NASENI).
“They were not allocated to them that they are now legal occupants. Those are collaborations,” he said.
Ugoh maintained that such partnerships were consistent with the university’s mandate to promote knowledge, research and institutional cooperation, rather than evidence of illegal land transfers.
However, he suggested that complications may have arisen when the EFCC reportedly sought to obtain a Certificate of Occupancy for the land despite the arrangement being a collaboration.
“I think what happened was that maybe somehow, the EFCC went and started looking for a Certificate of Occupancy for a collaboration, which wouldn’t have been in the first place. I think that is where the problem started,” he said.
On the wider controversy surrounding the disputed land, Ugoh challenged the FCTA’s justification for recovering undeveloped portions for urban development, alleging that the administration had instead transferred some portions to private interests.
He claimed that statutory rights of occupancy had been issued to individuals and companies, insisting that the documents were already in the public domain.
“The offer of right of occupancy, statutory right of occupancy, not just right of occupancy, issued to these individuals by the FCTA administration,” he said.
The ASUU chairman questioned why land belonging to a public university would be transferred to private beneficiaries, demanding transparency over the identities of the individuals and companies involved.
His clarification comes amid the wider controversy over the FCTA’s decision to reduce the university’s original 11,824 hectares of land, with the administration maintaining that its actions were based on recommendations of a joint committee.
The land dispute has generated protests by university staff, students and alumni, who are demanding a reversal of the decision and an end to further allocations.
Ugoh urged the authorities to distinguish between institutional collaborations and permanent land allocations, maintaining that partnerships with public institutions should not be used as grounds to question the university’s ownership of its property.
